named.name: Ceres
named.note: Largest object in the asteroid belt. Orbited by NASA's Dawn, 2015-2018.
named.discovery: Discovered 1801-01-01 by Piazzi, G. at Palermo

named.name: Vesta
named.note: Second-largest asteroid. Orbited by NASA's Dawn, 2011-2012.
named.discovery: Discovered 1807-03-29 by Olbers, H. W. at Bremen

named.name: Pallas
named.note: Third-largest asteroid, on a steeply tilted orbit.
named.discovery: Discovered 1802-03-28 by Olbers, H. W. at Bremen

named.name: Hygiea
named.note: Fourth-largest asteroid, and round enough that it may count as a dwarf planet.
named.discovery: Discovered 1849-04-12 by De Gasparis, A. at Naples

named.name: Juno
named.note: One of the first four asteroids found (1804).
named.discovery: Discovered 1804-09-01 by Harding, K. at Lilienthal

named.name: Psyche
named.note: A metal-rich asteroid. NASA's Psyche spacecraft is due to arrive in 2029.
named.discovery: Discovered 1852-03-17 by De Gasparis, A. at Naples

named.name: Eros
named.note: First asteroid orbited and landed on, by NASA's NEAR Shoemaker (2000-2001).
named.discovery: Discovered 1898-08-13 by Witt, G. at Berlin

named.name: Ida
named.note: First asteroid found to have a moon (Dactyl), in Galileo's images from 1993.
named.discovery: Discovered 1884-09-29 by Palisa, J. at Vienna

named.name: Gaspra
named.note: First asteroid visited by a spacecraft: Galileo flew past in 1991.
named.discovery: Discovered 1916-07-30 by Neujmin, G. at Simeis

named.name: Mathilde
named.note: A dark, carbon-rich asteroid. NEAR Shoemaker flew past in 1997.
named.discovery: Discovered 1885-11-12 by Palisa, J. at Vienna

named.name: Lutetia
named.note: ESA's Rosetta flew past in 2010.
named.discovery: Discovered 1852-11-15 by Goldschmidt, H. at Paris

named.name: Steins
named.note: ESA's Rosetta flew past in 2008.
named.discovery: Discovered 1969-11-04 by Chernykh, N. at Nauchnyj

named.name: Itokawa
named.note: Japan's Hayabusa brought back the first asteroid sample (2010).
named.discovery: Discovered 1998 Sept. 26 by the Lincoln Laboratory Near-Earth Asteroid Research Team at Socorro.
named.name_origin: Hideo Itokawa (1912-1999) is regarded as the Father of Japanese rocketry. An aerospace engineer, Itokawa initiated Japan's first launch tests of the solid rocket series called “Pencil” in 1955. Under his unique vision and strong leadership, his rockets reached space by 1960 and put Japan's first satellite into orbit in 1970.

named.name: Ryugu
named.note: Japan's Hayabusa2 brought samples back in 2020.
named.discovery: Discovered 1999 May 10 by the Lincoln Laboratory Near-Earth Asteroid Research Team at Socorro.
named.name_origin: Ryugu is the undersea palace of the Dragon God. In a Japanese legend, a fisherman was rewarded with a visit to Ryugu and brought back a box with a secret. The spaceprobe Hayabusa 2 will visit this asteroid and bring back a capsule containing surface samples.

named.name: Bennu
named.note: NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought samples back in 2023.
named.discovery: Discovered 1999 Sept. 11 by the Lincoln Laboratory Near-Earth Asteroid Research Team at Socorro.
named.name_origin: Bennu was an Egyptian mythological figure associated with Osiris, Atum and Ra. This minor planet is the target of the OSIRIS-REx sample return mission. OSIRIS-REx's Touch-and-Go Sampler evokes Bennu's image as a heron. Name suggested by Michael Toler Puzio (b. 2004) via a naming contest for students.

named.name: Apophis
named.note: Passes about 38,000 km from Earth's centre on 2029 April 13, inside the ring of geostationary satellites.
named.discovery: Discovered 2004 June 19 by R. A. Tucker, D. J. Tholen and F. Bernardi at Kitt Peak.
named.name_origin: Also known as Apep, the Destroyer, Apophis is the Egyptian god of evil and destruction who dwelled in eternal darkness. As a result of its passage within 40 000 km of the earth on 2029 Apr. 13, this minor planet will move from the Aten to the Apollo class.

named.name: Didymos
named.note: NASA's DART hit its moon Dimorphos in 2022 and changed its orbit: the first test of deflecting an asteroid.
named.discovery: Discovered 1996 Apr. 11 by Spacewatch at Kitt Peak.
named.name_origin: Greek for “twin”, this rapid-rotator Amor possesses a satellite with an orbital period of 11.9 hr. Suspicions arose in the Goldstone delay-Doppler echoes, and these were confirmed with the optical light curve analysis, along with Arecibo radar imaging on 2003 Nov. 23. The name was suggested by J. Montani.

named.name: Dinkinesh
named.note: NASA's Lucy flew past in 2023 and found its moon Selam is two lobes stuck together.
named.name_origin: Dinkinesh is an Ethiopian appellation for the Australopithecus afarensis skeleton AL 288-1, also known as “Lucy”, that was discovered in 1974 at Hadar, in the Awash Valley of Ethiopia. The nickname means “you are marvelous”.

named.name: Donaldjohanson
named.note: NASA's Lucy flew past in April 2025.
named.discovery: Discovered 1981 Mar. 2 by S. J. Bus at Siding Spring.
named.name_origin: American paleoanthropologist Donald Carl Johanson (b. 1943) discovered the fossil of a female hominin australopithecine known as ‘Lucy’.

named.name: Eurybates
named.note: A Jupiter Trojan. NASA's Lucy flies past in 2027.
named.discovery: Discovered 1973-09-19 by Van Houten, C. J. at Palomar

named.name: Patroclus
named.note: Two Trojan asteroids orbiting each other (with Menoetius). Lucy's last target, in 2033.
named.discovery: Discovered 1906-10-17 by Kopff, A. at Heidelberg

named.name: Phaethon
named.note: Parent of the Geminid meteor shower.
named.discovery: Discovered 1983-10-11 by IRAS at

named.name: Chiron
named.note: First centaur found (1977). It sometimes grows a coma like a comet.
named.discovery: Discovered 1977-10-18 by Kowal, C. at Palomar

named.name: Chariklo
named.note: Largest known centaur, and the first small body found to have rings (2013).
named.discovery: Discovered 1997 Feb. 15 by Spacewatch.
named.name_origin: Chariklo, sometimes described as a sea nymph, sometimes as a female centaur, was the wife of Chiron. Together they are said to have had as many as five children, and she is also sometimes said to have been the mother of Tiresias, the famous seer.

named.name: Eris
named.note: The most massive dwarf planet. Its discovery led to Pluto's reclassification in 2006.
named.discovery: Discovered 2003 Oct. 21 by M. E. Brown, C. A. Trujillo and D. Rabinowitz at Palomar.
named.name_origin: Eris is the Greek goddess of discord and strife. She stirs up jealousy and envy to cause fighting and anger among men. At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis all the gods were invited with the exception of Eris, and, enraged at her exclusion, she spitefully caused a quarrel among the goddesses that led to the Trojan war.

named.name: Haumea
named.note: Spins in about 4 hours, which stretches it into an egg shape. It has a ring.
named.size_note: Egg-shaped, 2,322 km long (drawn as a sphere of the same volume)
named.discovery: Discovered 2003 Mar. 7 at the Sierra Nevada Observatory.
named.name_origin: Haumea is the goddess of childbirth and fertility in Hawaiian mythology. Her many children sprang from different parts of her body. She takes many different forms and has experienced many different rebirths. As the goddess of the earth, she represents the element of stone. The satellites (136108) Haumea I and II were discovered by M. E. Brown, A. H. Bouchez and the Keck Observatory Adaptive Optics teams. Haumea I, discovered 2005 Jan. 26, is named Hi'iaka, who was born from the mouth of Haumea and carried by her sister Pele in egg form from their distant home to Hawaii. Hi'iaka danced the first Hula on the shores of Puna and is the patron goddess of the island of Hawaii and of hula dancers. Haumea II, discovered 2005 Nov. 7, is named Namaka, for a water spirit in Hawaiian mythology. Namaka was born from the body of Haumea and is the sister of Pele. When Pele sends her burning lava into the sea, Namaka cools the lava to become new land.

named.name: Makemake
named.note: The second-brightest Kuiper belt object, after Pluto.
named.discovery: Discovered 2005 Mar. 31 by M. E. Brown, C. A. Trujillo and D. L. Rabinowitz at Palomar.
named.name_origin: Makemake is the creator of humanity and the god of fertility in the mythology of the South Pacific island of Rapa Nui, or Easter Island. He was the chief god of the Tangata manu bird-man cult and was worshiped in the form of sea birds, which were his incarnation. His material symbol was a man with a bird's head.

named.name: Gonggong
named.note: One of the largest known objects beyond Neptune.
named.discovery: Discovered 2007 July 17 by M. E. Schwamb, M. E. Brown and D. Rabinowitz at Palomar.
named.name_origin: Gonggong is a Chinese water god with red hair and a serpent-like tail. He is known for creating chaos, causing flooding, and tilting the Earth; he is often depicted with the head of a human and the body of a snake. Gonggong is often attended by his minister, Xiangliu, a nine-headed poisonous snake monster for whom the satellite is named.

named.name: Quaoar
named.note: A large Kuiper belt object with a ring much farther out than rings should survive.
named.discovery: Discovered 2002 June 4 by C. A. Trujillo and M. E. Brown at Palomar.
named.name_origin: Quaoar is the great force of creation in the diverse myths of the Tongva, the indigenous people of the Los Angeles basin. Quaoar has no form or gender and dances and sings Weywot, Sky Father, into existence. Together, they create Chehooit, Earth Mother, and the trio bring Tamit, Grandfather Sun, to life.

named.name: Orcus
named.note: In the same 2:3 resonance with Neptune as Pluto, always on the opposite side of its orbit.
named.discovery: Discovered 2004 Feb. 17 by M. Brown, C. Trujillo and D. Rabinowitz
named.name_origin: Orcus was the Roman god of death, the counterpart of the Greek Pluto. Orcus collected the dead and carried them back to the underworld that he ruled.

named.name: Sedna
named.note: One of the most distant known objects in the Solar System, on a very elongated orbit.
named.discovery: Discovered 2003 Nov. 14 by M. E. Brown, C. A. Trujillo and D. Rabinowitz at Palomar.
named.name_origin: Sedna is the Inuit goddess of the sea and the mother of all sea creatures. She rewards the people of the land with food from the sea. Without her blessing, hunts fail and the people starve. She is thus one of the most important figures in Inuit legend.

named.name: Arrokoth
named.note: The most distant object visited by a spacecraft: New Horizons flew past in 2019.
named.size_note: 36 km long: two flattened lobes stuck together
named.discovery: Discovered 2014 by M. W. Buie and the New Horizons Search Team.
named.name_origin: Arrokoth is the word for “sky” from the Powhatan language of native people from the Chesapeake Bay region. Institutions in this region played a prominent role in facilitating the discovery and exploration of this ancient and distant object.

named.name: Halley's Comet
named.note: The most famous comet, back every ~76 years (next in 2061). Parent of the Eta Aquariid and Orionid meteor showers.
named.discovery: Discovered 1758-12-25 by Palitzsch, Johann Georg at

named.name: 2P/Encke
named.note: The shortest period of any bright comet: 3.3 years.
named.discovery: Discovered 1786-01-17 by Mechain, Pierre F. A. at

named.name: 9P/Tempel 1
named.note: NASA's Deep Impact fired an impactor into it in 2005.
named.discovery: Discovered 1867-04-03 by Tempel, William at Marseilles, France

named.name: 19P/Borrelly
named.note: NASA's Deep Space 1 flew past in 2001.
named.discovery: Discovered 1904-12-28 by Borrelly at Marseilles, France

named.name: 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko
named.note: Orbited by ESA's Rosetta (2014-2016). Its lander Philae touched down in 2014.
named.discovery: Discovered 1969-10-22 by Churyumov, Klim Ivanovic at Alma-Ata Observatory, Russia

named.name: 81P/Wild 2
named.note: NASA's Stardust brought dust from its coma back to Earth in 2006.
named.discovery: Discovered 1978-01-06 by Wild, Paul at Astronomical Institute of Berne, Switzerland

named.name: 103P/Hartley 2
named.note: NASA's EPOXI (the Deep Impact spacecraft) flew past in 2010.
named.discovery: Discovered 1986-03-15 by Hartley, Malcolm at U. K. Schmidt Telescope Unit, Siding Spring

named.name: 109P/Swift-Tuttle
named.note: Parent of the Perseid meteor shower.
named.discovery: Discovered 1862-07-16 by Swift, Lewis at Marathon, New York

named.name: 55P/Tempel-Tuttle
named.note: Parent of the Leonid meteor shower.
named.discovery: Discovered 1866-01-06 by Tuttle, Horace at Harvard College Observatory, Massachusetts

named.name: 12P/Pons-Brooks
named.note: Bright in 2024. Back every ~71 years.
named.discovery: Discovered 1812-07-21 by Pons, Jean Louis at Marseilles, France

named.name: Hale-Bopp
named.note: The Great Comet of 1997, visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months.

named.name: NEOWISE
named.note: The brightest comet in the northern sky since Hale-Bopp (July 2020).

named.name: Tsuchinshan-ATLAS
named.note: Bright in October 2024.

named.name: ʻOumuamua
named.note: The first known object from another star system (2017).

named.name: 2I/Borisov
named.note: The first known interstellar comet (2019).

named.name: 3I/ATLAS
named.note: The third known interstellar object, found in July 2025.
